title: L-M-D
hookLine: lamad, limmud, talmid, Talmud: learning and teaching share a root

lines: A LOUD ROOM, ONE OPEN PAGE.
cards: In a beit midrash, a house of study, the room is loud. Two people sit across from each other over one open page. One reads a line aloud.
The other says, no, that can't be what it means, and points at the next line. They push back and forth, sometimes for a long while on a few sentences. Who's the teacher here?
Watch long enough and it's hard to say. Each one is learning, and each one is teaching, often in the same breath. Hebrew has a root that refuses to keep those two apart.

teach.b: L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet. You met these letters as the example when the roots began: talmid, melamed, Talmud.
Today, what the root does. First, one verse, both ways.
At Horeb, God tells Moses to gather the people "that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and that they may teach their children."
Learn, and teach: the same three letters, a few words apart. Second, teach.
Later Moses says: "And ye shall teach them your children." The same root, in a form that means making someone else learn. Not two words: one root, facing two ways.

teach.h: THE TALMUD: A BOOK NAMED STUDY.
teach.b: The collection of rabbinic study, argument and story is called the Talmud, from these same letters. Its name is study. Fourth, who learns from whom.

teach.h: MOST OF ALL FROM MY STUDENTS.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, records Rabbi Chanina saying he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and from his students most of all. And the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, asks: who is wise?

The one who learns from every person. So the teacher is always also a student, and the arrow points either way across the table. Even Isaiah uses the root in his picture of peace: "neither shall they learn war any more."
What people learn, they can also unlearn.

how: Jews study Torah and Talmud in houses of study, synagogues and homes, often in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and arguing over each line together.

o: a root that means to read words aloud
one root for both learning and teaching
a root that means to argue or debate

games.q: one root, two directions — tap the pairs.
p: one verse at Horeb, one root
one who learns from every person

s: in Hebrew, learn and teach come from different roots
both are lamed, mem, dalet. teaching is making someone else learn.
Rabbi Chanina said he learned the most from his students
tractate Taanit: much from teachers, more from friends, most from students.
Pirkei Avot says the wise one learns only from the wise
the wise one learns from every person.

games.q: you're the teacher in a study hall. a student challenges your reading of a line, and has a point. what does this root suggest?
o: defend your reading to keep your authority.
move on to the next line.
games.why: in tractate Taanit, Rabbi Chanina says he learned most of all from his students. in this root, teaching and learning run both ways.

practice: Look back over these roots: shalom, wholeness; bracha, blessing that bends; emet, truth with its first letter; shema, hearing that heeds; teshuvah, turning.
Pick the one that stuck and shape it into a single sentence you could say plainly over dinner, with no notes. If you pray, you can bring that sentence into your prayer as something learned.

wordCard.voice: L-M-D. Lamed, mem, dalet: to learn and to teach. The letters of talmid, student, and of the Talmud. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a student; from the root lamed, mem, dalet, to learn and to teach.
